note.subject: science

Putting energy on the arrow, as in the photosynthesis equation
Answering 'give two uses of the energy' with 'to produce energy' (Summer 2025, both tiers)

Claiming a plant respires only at night
Using the final temperature as the temperature rise
Describing active transport as moving substances down the concentration gradient (Higher)

noteBlocks.lede: Respiration is how a living cell gets the energy it needs out of food. Oxygen and glucose go in, energy comes out, and carbon dioxide and water are what is left. It runs in every cell, day and night, and a flask of sprouting peas warms up because of it.

Give two uses of the released energy, and explain the boiled-pea control.

noteBlocks.text: Aerobic respiration: the reaction every cell is doing right now

noteBlocks.md: Every cell in you is doing this reaction right now, and it does not stop while you sleep. Glucose from your food meets oxygen from your breath, and the energy stored in the glucose is released for warmth, movement and growth. Carbon dioxide and water are left over.

noteBlocks.alt: The word equation glucose plus oxygen gives energy plus carbon dioxide plus water, and beneath it the balanced symbol equation C6H12O6 plus 6O2 gives energy plus 6CO2 plus 6H2O, marked Higher Tier. A two-row table underneath contrasts photosynthesis, where energy sits on the arrow as a condition and the reaction is endothermic, with respiration, where energy is written as a product and the reaction is exothermic.

noteBlocks.explain: Water. Three products, and CCEA writes 'energy' as the first of them — unlike photosynthesis, where energy goes on the arrow.

noteBlocks.title: Why energy is written differently in the two equations
noteBlocks.md: Photosynthesis **takes energy in**, so light is a condition that has to be supplied — it goes on the arrow. Respiration **gives energy out**, so CCEA writes energy among the products. That is the difference between **endothermic** and **exothermic** in one line of layout, and it is why 'energy' belongs in a box here and never in the photosynthesis equation.

noteBlocks.prompt: Respiration is described as exothermic. What does that tell you?
noteBlocks.explain: Exo means out. That is why a bag of germinating seeds warms up, and it is a Higher Tier clause in this outcome.

noteBlocks.md: **Where, and how often.** Respiration happens in the **mitochondria**, in **every living cell**, **all the time** — plants included, day and night. It does not stop when you sleep and it does not stop in a leaf in the light. That last point is what the hydrogencarbonate-indicator questions in B1 are really testing.

noteBlocks.title: GCSE Biology Revision "Respiration"
noteBlocks.why: Five minutes on aerobic respiration, the equation and why the reaction is exothermic. Watch it, then answer the question underneath without scrolling back.

noteBlocks.prompt: In which organelle does aerobic respiration take place?
noteBlocks.explain: The mitochondria. This clause is printed in bold in the specification, which marks it Higher Tier — but it is one word, so learn it either way.

noteBlocks.md: The specification lists five: **heat**, **movement**, **growth**, **reproduction** and **active uptake/transport** (the last is Higher Tier). When a question says 'respiration releases energy — give two uses for that energy', it has already given you the release. The marks are for what the body spends it on.

noteBlocks.title: Summer 2025 B1 Foundation Q7 and B1 Higher Q2
noteBlocks.md: The same QWC question ran on both tiers. Some answers had the carbon dioxide the wrong way round — **taken in rather than given out**. Others wrote that respiration releases energy, which the question had already told them; the marks were for **what the body does with it**. The scheme gave no top band without **at least one named use**.

noteBlocks.prompt: A question asks for two uses of the energy released in respiration. Which answer earns both marks?
options: to produce energy, and to stay alive
noteBlocks.explain: Two of the five named uses. 'To produce energy' repeats the question, and glucose and oxygen are the reactants, not uses.

noteBlocks.md: Put germinating peas in a vacuum flask with a thermometer, and boiled (dead) peas in an identical one. After 3 days the living peas have warmed from 22.5 °C to 27.0 °C — a rise of 4.5 °C. The dead peas rose only from 22.5 °C to 22.8 °C, a rise of 0.3 °C. The living peas are respiring; the boiled ones cannot, so the extra 4.2 °C must come from respiration. That is the evidence that respiration is **exothermic**.

noteBlocks.prompt: The living peas warmed from 22.5 °C to 27.0 °C. What was the temperature rise, in °C?
noteBlocks.explain: 27.0 − 22.5 = 4.5 °C. Always give the rise, not the final reading.

noteBlocks.title: Why flask B is not a waste of peas
noteBlocks.md: Flask B is the **control**. It is identical in every way except that its peas are dead, so it shows that the temperature rise in flask A was caused by the **living** peas and not by the room warming up, the cotton wool or the flask itself. A control changes exactly one thing — and boiling the peas is how you change 'alive' without changing anything else.

noteBlocks.prompt: Why were the peas in flask B boiled before the experiment?
options: To kill them, so they could not respire
To remove the water from them
noteBlocks.answer: To kill them, so they could not respire
noteBlocks.explain: Dead peas cannot respire, so flask B shows what happens with everything else the same and respiration removed.

noteBlocks.md:
Write the **word equation**, with energy among the products.
Name the **mitochondria** as the site of the reaction.
Give **two uses** of the energy released.
Explain why living peas warm a flask and boiled peas do not.

Six to nine marks, and in most series this is the paper's six-mark QWC. Expect the word equation into boxes, the organelle named, two uses of the energy, and a data part on a temperature rise or a limewater result. Write **released**, never made: energy is not created. Stuck: write the equation out, because each box is a mark.

steps.decision: Start with what goes in. Glucose is the fuel and oxygen is what burns it; both are used up, so both are on the left.
Carbon dioxide is made, not used — that is the exact confusion Summer 2025's examiners reported. Water is the product candidates most often leave out.

options: Because respiration is the reverse of photosynthesis in what it uses and makes
Because carbon dioxide is a gas
Because water is always a product
whyMenu.explain: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and makes oxygen; respiration uses oxygen and makes carbon dioxide. Holding the pair together fixes both.

steps.working: glucose + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water
steps.decision: Energy stays on the product side because respiration is exothermic. In photosynthesis it would go on the arrow instead.

steps.working: The student had the reaction backwards: they wrote the reactants of photosynthesis as the reactants of respiration.
steps.decision: Name the error. A question that asks you to explain the change wants the diagnosis, not just the corrected line.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: glucose + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water. Oxygen and glucose are used up, so they are reactants; carbon dioxide and water are made, so they are products; and energy is written as a product because respiration is exothermic.

items.stem: In aerobic respiration, is carbon dioxide used or produced?
items.skill: Get the direction of each gas right

options.text: Produced — it is one of the products
options.feedback: Oxygen in, carbon dioxide out. Summer 2025 examiners named this confusion in the QWC question on both tiers.

options.text: Used — it is one of the reactants
options.feedback: That is photosynthesis. Respiration uses oxygen and makes carbon dioxide.

options.text: Neither — carbon dioxide is not involved
options.feedback: It is a product, and it is what limewater detects in a respiration experiment.

options.text: Both, in equal amounts
options.feedback: A substance appears on one side of an equation, not both.

items.stem: A question asks for two uses of the energy released by respiration. Which answer scores?
items.skill: Give uses of the energy, not a restatement

options.text: Growth and active transport
options.feedback: Two of the five named uses: heat, movement, growth, reproduction and active uptake or transport.

options.text: To make energy and to produce ATP
options.feedback: The first repeats the question and the second is not on this specification. Summer 2025 examiners reported exactly this.

options.text: Glucose and oxygen
options.feedback: Those are the reactants of respiration, not what the energy is used for.

options.text: Breathing and heart rate
options.feedback: Those are responses to a need for energy, not the specification's list of uses.

items.stem: Where does aerobic respiration take place in a cell?

options.text: In the mitochondria
options.feedback: In the mitochondria, in every living cell, all the time.

options.text: In the lungs
options.feedback: The lungs are where breathing happens. Respiration is a chemical reaction inside cells, and the question asks about a cell.

options.text: In the chloroplasts
options.feedback: Chloroplasts are for photosynthesis. Plants have mitochondria too, and they respire in them.

options.text: In the nucleus
options.feedback: The nucleus holds the chromosomes. Respiration happens in the mitochondria.

items.stem: Which statement about respiration in a plant is correct?
items.skill: Recall that respiration is continuous in all cells

options.text: A plant respires all the time, day and night
options.feedback: Continuously, in every living cell. In the light it photosynthesises as well, which is a different reaction.

options.text: A plant only respires at night
options.feedback: It respires at night too, but not only then. Photosynthesis is the one that needs light.

options.text: A plant respires only in its leaves
options.feedback: Every living cell respires, including root and stem cells that never see light.

options.text: A plant does not respire, it photosynthesises instead
options.feedback: It does both. Photosynthesis makes the glucose; respiration releases the energy from it.

items.stem: Respiration is exothermic. Which piece of evidence shows this?

options.text: A flask of germinating peas warms up while a flask of boiled peas does not
options.feedback: Heat released, with a control to show it came from the living peas.

options.text: The peas use up the oxygen in the flask
options.feedback: True, but that shows oxygen is a reactant, not that energy is released as heat.

options.text: The peas grow taller
options.feedback: Growth is one use of the energy, but the word exothermic is about energy given out as heat.

options.text: Limewater turns milky
options.feedback: That shows carbon dioxide is produced. The temperature rise is what shows the reaction is exothermic.

energy
carbon dioxide

parts.stem:
A pupil says: 'Plants photosynthesise in the day and respire at night.'
Explain why this is not correct.

accepted: plants respire all the time, day and night, in every living cell; in the light they photosynthesise as well

scheme.for: respiration happens continuously, day and night
in every living cell, including roots that never receive light
in the light the plant photosynthesises as well, so both reactions run at once

hints: Which of the two reactions actually needs light?
Think about a root cell, which never sees any light at all.
parts.workedSolution: Respiration happens continuously in every living cell of the plant, day and night — root cells never see light and still respire. What stops in the dark is photosynthesis. In the light the plant does both at once, and what you measure from outside is only the difference between them.

pattern.regex: only at night|stops in the light

commonErrors.feedback: Respiration never stops. Photosynthesis is the reaction that needs light.

context.setting: Two vacuum flasks of peas left in a cupboard for three days

figures.alt: Two vacuum flasks with thermometers, one holding living germinating peas and one holding peas that were boiled and then cooled.

parts.stem:
Flask A held living peas and warmed from 22.5 °C to 27.0 °C.
Calculate the temperature rise in flask A.

scheme.examinerNote: Unit needed; both readings are to one decimal place, so the answer is too.

hints: Final temperature minus starting temperature.

commonErrors.feedback: 27.0 °C is the final temperature, not the rise. Subtract the start.

parts.stem: Explain why the peas in flask B were boiled before the experiment.

accepted: boiling kills the peas so they cannot respire, making flask B a control

scheme.for: boiling kills the peas, so they cannot respire
so flask B is a control: it shows the temperature rise in flask A was caused by the living peas and not by the room or the flask

hints: Two marks: what boiling does, and why that makes the experiment mean something.
parts.workedSolution: Boiling kills the peas so they can no longer respire. Flask B is then identical to flask A in every way except that respiration is not happening, so it acts as a control and shows the rise in A was caused by the living peas.

commonErrors.feedback: Repeats give reliability; a control shows what caused the change. Flask B is a control.

parts.stem:
Flask B rose by 0.3 °C.
Explain why the results show that respiration is exothermic.

accepted: the living peas warmed far more than the dead ones, so respiration must be releasing heat

scheme.for: flask A rose by 4.5 °C compared with only 0.3 °C in flask B
scheme.examinerNote: A comparison must quote both values.

scheme.for: so the respiring peas released energy as heat — the reaction is exothermic

hints: Quote both rises, then say what the difference means.
parts.workedSolution: Flask A rose by 4.5 °C while flask B, with everything the same except that its peas were dead, rose by only 0.3 °C. The extra 4.2 °C must have come from the living peas respiring, so respiration releases energy as heat and is exothermic.

commonErrors.feedback: No values quoted. CCEA's schemes ask for comparisons with the data where data is given.

context.setting: The same flask of germinating peas, measured over three days

parts.stem:

Calculate the mean temperature rise per day.
Show your working out.

scheme.for: 1.5 (°C per day)
scheme.examinerNote: Units needed. Correct answer with unit is worth [2].

hints: A mean per day is the total change divided by the number of days.

commonErrors.feedback: 4.5 °C is the whole rise over three days, not the rise per day. Divide by 3.

parts.stem:
A student breathes out through limewater and it turns milky. Another student says this proves respiration is happening in the lungs.
Explain why the second student is wrong.

accepted: respiration happens in the cells, in the mitochondria; the lungs only exchange the gases that the blood brings

scheme.for: respiration is a chemical reaction that takes place inside cells, in the mitochondria
the lungs carry out gas exchange: the carbon dioxide is brought there by the blood from the respiring cells

hints: Separate the two words: breathing moves air; respiration is a reaction in cells.
parts.workedSolution: Respiration is a chemical reaction that happens inside cells, in the mitochondria, all over the body. The carbon dioxide is carried to the lungs by the blood, and the lungs only exchange it with the air. Breathing and respiration are different things.

commonErrors.feedback: The lungs are where gas exchange happens. Respiration happens in the mitochondria of cells.

context.setting: A root hair cell taking up nitrate ions from the soil

parts.stem:
Complete the balanced equation for aerobic respiration.

C₆H₁₂O₆ + ______  →  energy + 6CO₂ + ______

scheme.for: 6O₂
6H₂O

hints: Balance the hydrogens first: twelve in the glucose means six waters.

parts.stem: State the type of reaction respiration is, in terms of energy.

scheme.for: exothermic

commonErrors.feedback: Endothermic is photosynthesis, which takes energy in. Respiration gives energy out.

parts.stem:
Nitrate ions are more concentrated inside a root hair cell than in the soil water outside it, yet the cell continues to take them in.
Explain how respiration makes this possible.

accepted: the ions are moved by active transport against the concentration gradient, which needs energy released by respiration

scheme.for: the nitrate ions are taken in by active transport / active uptake
against the concentration gradient, from a lower to a higher concentration
which requires energy released by respiration in the cell's mitochondria

hints: Diffusion only works one way — down a gradient. This is going the other way.
Active uptake is one of the five uses of energy the specification lists.
parts.workedSolution: Nitrate ions are taken in by active transport, which moves them against the concentration gradient from the lower concentration in the soil water to the higher concentration inside the cell. Moving a substance against a gradient needs energy, and that energy is released by respiration in the cell's mitochondria.

commonErrors.feedback: Diffusion moves substances down a gradient and needs no energy. Here the ions move against the gradient, which is why respiration is involved.

context.setting: A seedling growing in the dark from the food stored in its seed

parts.stem:
A seedling germinating in a dark cupboard grows taller and feels slightly warm.
Describe the process of aerobic respiration in the seedling's cells.
Give two uses of the energy released.
Your written communication is assessed in this question, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; organised clearly; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: it takes place in the mitochondria and is exothermic, releasing energy continuously
one use of the energy: growth, building new cells
a second use: heat to keep warm, movement, reproduction or active uptake

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Name all four substances and say for each whether it is used or produced — that is where Summer 2025's candidates went wrong.
You must give at least one use of the energy to reach the top band, and 'to produce energy' is not a use.
parts.workedSolution: In the seedling's cells, glucose from the food stored in the seed reacts with oxygen. The reaction takes place in the mitochondria and produces carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy as it goes: it is exothermic, and it happens continuously in every living cell. The seedling uses that energy for growth, building new cells so that it gets taller, and as heat, which is why the seedling feels slightly warm.

pattern.regex: carbon dioxide is used|uses carbon dioxide

commonErrors.feedback: Carbon dioxide is produced by respiration, not used. Summer 2025 examiners reported this confusion on both tiers of this QWC question.
No use of the energy has been given, and the mark scheme requires at least one to reach the top band. 'It produces energy' restates the question.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ruairí is asked: 'Describe the process of aerobic respiration and give two uses for the energy released. [6]'
His answer:
studentWorking: Aerobic respiration happens in the lungs.
It uses oxygen and carbon dioxide to make glucose and water.
The energy released is used to produce energy for the body.
It is also used to keep you alive.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 has the reaction running backwards: it uses carbon dioxide and makes glucose, which is photosynthesis. Respiration uses glucose and oxygen and makes carbon dioxide and water. Lines 3 and 4 then give no use of the energy at all — 'to produce energy' repeats the question and 'to keep you alive' is not one of the five the specification names.
correction: Aerobic respiration happens in the mitochondria of every living cell.
It uses glucose and oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy.
The energy released is used for movement, such as muscle contraction.
It is also used for growth, building new cells.
findTheMistake.feedback: This sits in Band C. One indicative point survives — oxygen is involved — and the writing is clear, which is what keeps it off zero. The two repairs are small and worth three or four marks between them: turn line 2 round so carbon dioxide is on the product side, and replace lines 3 and 4 with two of the five named uses. Summer 2025's report describes both errors in the same paragraph, so they are worth practising together.

prompts.prompt: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
prompts.answer: glucose + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water

prompts.prompt: Write the balanced symbol equation for aerobic respiration. (Higher)
In which equation does 'energy' go on the arrow, and in which is it written as a product?
prompts.answer: On the arrow in photosynthesis, which is endothermic and needs light supplied. As a product in respiration, which is exothermic and gives energy out.

prompts.prompt: Name the five uses of the energy released by respiration.
prompts.answer: Heat, movement, growth, reproduction, and active uptake or transport.

prompts.prompt: Where and how often does respiration happen?
prompts.answer: In the mitochondria, in every living cell, continuously — day and night, in plants as well as animals.

prompts.prompt: What is the difference between breathing and respiration?
prompts.answer: Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs. Respiration is a chemical reaction inside cells, in the mitochondria, that releases energy from glucose.

prompts.prompt: A flask of germinating peas warms up but a flask of boiled peas does not. What does that show, and what is the second flask for?
prompts.answer: Respiration is exothermic — it releases energy as heat. The boiled peas are the control, showing the rise was caused by the living peas and not by the surroundings.

prompts.prompt: Why does active transport need respiration?
prompts.answer: Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient, which needs energy, and that energy is released by respiration.
